name: libxml2-wasm
language: C (libxml2) compiled to WebAssembly with Emscripten; TypeScript wrapper
baseline: libxmljs2 0.32.x (native N-API binding of libxml2) and the pure-JavaScript XML parsers @rgrove/parse-xml, fast-xml-parser and xmldoc
workload: DOM-tree parse of three XML fixtures (780 B, 35,562 B and 2,337,522 B) under Node.js, via the benchmark/ suite in the repo (cd benchmark && npm install && npm test).
claimed_speedup: Buffer API vs native libxmljs2: 167,479 vs 78,688 ops/s on the 780 B file (2.1x, derived from page data), 17,114 vs 12,414 on 35,562 B (1.4x, derived), 62 vs 50 on 2.3 MB (1.2x, derived). String API: 120,578 vs 78,688 ops/s on the small file (1.5x, derived) but 6,013 vs 12,414 (medium) and 43 vs 50 (large), i.e. slower than the native binding. Both APIs beat the pure-JS parsers (large file: 62 and 43 ops/s vs @rgrove/parse-xml 19, fast-xml-parser 16, xmldoc 11).
compiler_and_flags: Emscripten (emcc, linked with @binding/emcc.txt, not read); libxml2 configured via emconfigure with CFLAGS='-O2' --without-sax1 --without-modules --without-html --without-threads --without-catalog --without-debug --disable-shared --enable-static (package.json scripts). Build flags of the libxmljs2 baseline are not stated.
hardware: Apple M3 Max (Darwin arm64), Node.js v18.19.0
stars_or_usage: 54 stars; published on npm as libxml2-wasm
tradeoffs: ES module only; needs Node.js 18+ or Chrome/Edge 89+, Safari 15+ (README). libxml2 is built without the HTML parser, SAX1, catalogs, threads, modules and debug support. The String API converts UTF-16 to UTF-8 on every call; the docs recommend the Buffer API for speed. Wrapper licence is MIT and the bundled libxml2 keeps its own notice (LICENSE.libxml2).
caveats: Wins over the native binding only with the Buffer API and by a shrinking margin as documents grow (2.1x, 1.4x, 1.2x); the String API loses to libxmljs2 on the medium and large files. DOM parse only, one run on the maintainer's laptop with an old Node.js 18.19.0; the results block in docs/performance.md is undated and not repeated on x86. libxmljs2 is a prebuilt/node-gyp binding whose compiler flags are unstated. The README's own speed row is qualitative ('Fast').
found_via: WebSearch result app.unpkg.com/libxml2-wasm README (query on wasm libraries faster than JS builtins); then opened github.com/jameslan/libxml2-wasm and docs/performance.md

name: lz4-wasm
language: Rust (lz4_flex) compiled to WebAssembly with wasm-pack
baseline: 'lz4 js' (a pure-JavaScript LZ4 block implementation; the package is not named in the README) and fflate (deflate)
workload: LZ4 block compression and decompression of four inputs (66 kB JSON, 65 kB text, 34 kB text, 1 kB text) in a browser, with compression ratio.
claimed_speedup: Tagline: compress 200 MB/s Firefox and 350 MB/s Chrome, decompress 600 MB/s Firefox and 1400 MB/s Chrome. Table, wasm vs lz4 js: 66k JSON compress 292.43 vs 101.48 MB/s (2.9x, derived from page data), decompress 687.37 vs 27.06 MB/s (25x, derived); 65k text 146.10 vs 73.55 (2.0x) and 610.59 vs 28.15 (22x); 34k text 159.57 vs 59.77 (2.7x) and 562.43 vs 28.10 (20x); 1k text 181.25 vs 2.18 (83x) and 362.50 vs 45.31 (8x).
compiler_and_flags: RUST_LOG=info wasm-pack build --release (README); no other flags stated
stars_or_usage: 16 stars; npm packages lz4-wasm and lz4-wasm-nodejs
tradeoffs: Uses the LZ4 block API and prepends the original length as a 32-bit little-endian value, so output is not the LZ4 frame format and is not readable by the lz4 CLI. No streaming API; only compress and decompress on Uint8Array. Lower ratio than fflate (0.23 vs 0.17 on 66 kB JSON).
caveats: No CPU model, browser versions or run counts stated; the live demo page (pseitz.github.io/lz4-wasm) was not reachable here. The 1 kB lz4 js row (2.18 MB/s, 83x gap) looks dominated by warm-up. fflate is a different algorithm with a better ratio, so its rows are a context comparison. The package is a wasm packaging of lz4_flex, which is already catalogued, so a verifier may fold it as a duplicate. Last commit 2023-06-24.
found_via: npm registry lookup of lz4-wasm (README points at the lz4_flex repo), then raw README and github.com/PSeitz/lz4-wasm and /commits

name: swisseph-wasm
language: Rust FFI over C (Swiss Ephemeris 2.10.03) compiled to WebAssembly
workload: Moon position (Deno bench) and Sun position (Chrome and Deno) calculations, wasm Swiss Ephemeris vs astronomy-engine.
claimed_speedup: Moon position: ~182,000 iter/s vs ~126,000 iter/s for astronomy-engine, '1.44x Faster' (Deno bench). Sun position is slower: ~319,000 vs ~577,000 ops/s in Chrome and ~178,000 vs ~434,000 ops/s in Deno ('the overhead of calling WebAssembly dominates. Pure JS is faster here').
stars_or_usage: 4 stars; JSR, npm and crates.io badges in README
tradeoffs: Bundles the Swiss Ephemeris C library, which the README describes as GPL/Commercial dual licensed, while the wrapper code is MIT, so redistribution inherits the ephemeris terms. Boundary-call overhead makes simple calls slower than pure JS.
caveats: One winning row (Moon) against two losing rows (Sun); the README says swisseph-wasm is also more accurate, so the two libraries do different amounts of work per call. No CPU, Deno or Chrome versions stated. Reproducible with 'deno task bench' in the repo, but not run here.
found_via: crates.io API sweep (query 'wasm faster than javascript') then raw README of fusionstrings/swisseph-wasm and github.com page and /commits

name: Orlando (orlando-transducers)
baseline: native JavaScript Array methods (map/filter chains); also compared with Lazy.js, Lodash, Underscore and Ramda
workload: Five transducer-pipeline scenarios under Node.js: map-filter-take over 100K items, a 10-operation pipeline over 50K items, find-first-5 over 1M items, object processing over 500K items, simple map over 1M items.
claimed_speedup: README: '3-19x speedup' over native array methods (Performance table 2.3 ms vs 0.6 ms = 3.8x; 8.7 ms vs 2.1 ms = 4.1x; 15.2 ms vs 0.8 ms = 19x). BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md, M1 Max: map-filter-take 18,234 ops/s vs 3,801 native (4.8x), complex pipeline 1,234 vs 389 (3.2x), early termination 24,391 vs 1,304 (18.7x), object processing 234 vs 84 (2.8x); simple map 687 vs 891 ops/s (Orlando 1.3x slower).
compiler_and_flags: npm run build:nodejs (wasm-bindgen build); no Rust or wasm-opt flags stated
hardware: Apple M1 Max (10 cores), 32 GB, Node.js v20.11.0; also i7-12700K Ubuntu and a 2-core GitHub Actions Xeon (Node v20.11.0 / v20.x)
tradeoffs: Pipelines must be built through Orlando's Pipeline API after an async wasm init(), not Array.prototype chains; data crosses the JS/WASM boundary; slower than native arrays for a single simple map.
caveats: The win is mostly algorithmic (no intermediate arrays, early termination), not wasm code generation: pure-JS Lazy.js is within 1.2x of Orlando in the same table (22,134 vs 24,391 ops/s on early termination). The results file calls itself 'Sample benchmark results', does not say whether the figures were measured or illustrative, and is dated 2025-01-22, before the repo's visible 2026 history; the round numbers across three environments are unusual. The README's Performance table and Benchmarks section give different figures. Repository moved from justinelliottcobb/Orlando to Industrial-Algebra/Orlando.
found_via: crates.io API sweep (query 'wasm faster than javascript') then github.com/Industrial-Algebra/Orlando README, benchmarks/BENCHMARK_RESULTS.md and /commits

name: d3_geo_voronoi_rs (rust_d3_geo_voronoi)
baseline: d3-geo-voronoi (the original JavaScript library, github.com/Fil/d3-geo-voronoi), run on an equivalent benchmark web page
workload: Frames-per-second style browser benchmark: Delaunay/Voronoi mesh of random points on a sphere rendered each frame; points rendered within a 16 ms frame budget.
claimed_speedup: JavaScript renders 600 points in 16 ms at the tuned 60 fps setting; the Rust version does the same workload in 8.165 ms (README: 'a factor 1.95 speedup'), and renders 1220 points in 16 ms, 'an increase of just under 2'.
compiler_and_flags: wasm-pack, built with 'npm run build' in benchmark/www for best performance; Rust flags not stated
tradeoffs: Port is incomplete (contour.js not ported); README says the demo works only with f64 because f32 breaks cell integrity.
caveats: Single author measurement with no CPU, browser or run counts. The README notes a failing test ('geoVoronoi.hull does not break on difficult polygons'). The licence is MIT in Cargo.toml but the repository has no LICENSE file. The wasm bundle also includes the Rust ports of d3-geo and d3-delaunay, so the comparison is whole-pipeline, not just the Voronoi step. README text about the benchmark running in the browser is implied by the wasm-pack build steps, not stated outright.
found_via: crates.io API sweep (query 'wasm faster than javascript'); opened github.com/martinfrances107/rust_d3_geo_voronoi, its README, benchmark/README.md and /commits

name: spow
language: Rust (server crate, browser WASM and JS-only solvers)
baseline: the JS-only browser solver shipped in prebuilt/browser, and optimised native Rust (the wasm build is slower than native)
workload: Time to solve a proof-of-work puzzle (Hashcat-style PoW, difficulty 10-99, default 20) in the browser: WASM solver vs JS-only solver vs native Rust.
claimed_speedup: README: the wasm version 'is up to ~20 times faster than JS only'; 'the JS version is ~20 times slower than wasm'; in the browser the wasm version needs 'roughly 2.5 - 3 times the amount of time' of optimised native Rust ('first tests').
tradeoffs: Solve time grows exponentially with difficulty (10-99); wasm needs a getrandom backend setting in .cargo/config.toml; server-side validation time is independent of difficulty.
caveats: The README gives ratios only ('first tests'), with no table, hardware, browser, difficulty or sample count. A benches/ directory and a median-solve-time bin target exist in the repo but were not read. The wasm build is itself 2.5-3x slower than native Rust, so it beats only the JS baseline.
found_via: crates.io API sweep (query 'wasm faster than javascript') then raw README of sebadob/spow and github.com page and /commits

name: authia
baseline: jose (JavaScript JOSE library: WebCrypto on Cloudflare Workers, native Node.js crypto bindings on Node)
workload: Ed25519 JWT verification per call on Cloudflare Workers / edge runtimes and on Node.js.
claimed_speedup: Cloudflare Workers: authia (WASM) 0.20 ms avg, 0.17 ms p50, 0.36 ms p95 vs jose (WebCrypto) 0.30 / 0.28 / 0.50 ms (avg 1.5x lower, derived from page data). Node.js: jose (native crypto) 0.01-0.03 ms vs authia 0.17-0.20 ms, so the wasm build is 6-20x slower there (derived).
tradeoffs: Ed25519 JWT verification only; WASM must be initialised; slower than native crypto on Node.js (README says so).
caveats: Honest mixed result: the README itself says jose is significantly faster on Node.js and recommends authia for edge runtimes. No CPU, runtime versions, iteration counts or jose version stated; a benches/ directory exists but was not read. Repository moved from Taniyama2024/authia to HaradaTakuma/authia.
found_via: crates.io API sweep (query 'wasm faster than javascript', crate 'authia'); opened github.com/HaradaTakuma/authia README and /commits

name: sanity-lint (groq-wasm)
language: Rust (groq-lint, groq-format) compiled to WebAssembly; TypeScript
baseline: TypeScript implementation of the same GROQ lint rules (the automatic fallback in @sanity-labs/groq-lint; README names no baseline)
workload: Linting of pure GROQ rules; workload, corpus and measurement not described.
claimed_speedup: README: 'Linting: Pure GROQ rules run via Rust/WASM (~5-10x faster)'.
tradeoffs: Falls back to the TypeScript rules automatically when WASM is unavailable; the WASM bindings wrap atombender/groq-lint and groq-format.
caveats: Single sentence claim with no benchmark, workload, hardware or method; the top-level listing shows no benchmark directory and packages/groq-wasm was not inspected. Baseline is inferred from the stated TypeScript fallback.
found_via: npm registry search (keywords wasm, fast) then raw README and github.com/sanity-labs/sanity-lint and /commits
